Summary and definitions
- An “alkaline diet” typically emphasizes minimally processed plant foods (fruits, vegetables, legumes, whole grains) that are proposed to leave an alkalinizing metabolic residue (alkaline ash) after metabolism, whereas a “traditional” Western-style pattern often includes more refined grains, added sugars, and animal products, producing a more acidogenic load metabolically. <cite id="fa31949a-1">Because the Mediterranean-style diet is more plant-based, higher in fibre and lower in meats and dairy, it has potential to be less acidic; limited research has reported positive effects of alkaline diets on lean muscle mass in healthy older adults</cite>. 
- Muscle mass retention and muscle protein synthesis (MPS) depend on protein intake quality and quantity, leucine signaling (mTOR), energy balance and exercise, and the net effect of protein degradation pathways; age blunts the anabolic response to amino acids unless leucine/EAAs are provided adequately. <cite id="da90c754-0">BCAAs (especially leucine) act as substrates for protein synthesis, as signaling molecules to stimulate protein synthesis, and as energy substrates; aging reduces anabolism and insulin/AA responsiveness but BCAAs, particularly leucine, can still stimulate MPS</cite> <cite id="59bac8a5-3">Muscle growth is controlled by a balance between synthesis and degradation, with notable sensitivity of muscle protein degradation to nutritional factors</cite> <cite id="da90c754-2">Ample essential amino acids and leucine are required to elicit a muscle anabolic response in older adults, with the anabolic “muscle-full” period limiting leucine’s effects shortly after meals</cite>.

Mechanisms linking diet type to muscle outcomes
- Diet-induced acidosis may favor proteolysis and impair net accretion unless countered by sufficient alkaline minerals and amino acids; conversely, plant-rich alkaline-ash patterns may mitigate acid load while providing fiber and phytochemicals that reduce inflammation and oxidative stress that otherwise degrade muscle. <cite id="fa31949a-1">The Mediterranean pattern (more plant-based, lower meat/dairy) is potentially less acidic, and has been reported to positively affect lean muscle mass in healthy older adults</cite>. 
- Leucine uniquely activates mTOR-dependent translation initiation, increasing MPS when available; effects depend on maintaining elevated amino acid pools and are blunted with age unless sufficient EAAs/leucine are provided per meal. <cite id="e05199ed-0">In protein-restricted adult rats, leucine supplementation increased skeletal muscle protein synthesis and phosphorylation of 4E-BP1 and S6K1 via mTOR, and increased gastrocnemius weight vs control and alanine-supplemented groups</cite> <cite id="e05199ed-3">Long-term leucine infusion in neonates increased mTOR activation in skeletal muscle and some visceral tissues, but protein synthesis rose only when baseline amino acids were maintained, illustrating the requirement for sustained amino acid availability</cite> <cite id="e05199ed-4">In young men, a leucine-rich solution increased muscle protein synthesis and phosphorylation of Akt/mTOR and reduced AMPK, consistent with enhanced translation initiation</cite> <cite id="da90c754-0">Leucine can reverse impaired MPS in elderly subjects, though younger adults show smaller incremental benefits</cite>. 
- Protein quality matters: plant proteins are often lower in lysine, methionine, and leucine, requiring higher amounts or complementary blends to match animal protein’s anabolic signaling, especially in older adults. <cite id="fa31949a-0">Older adults may respond differently to MPS after plant- vs omnivorous meals; plant protein’s lower anabolic properties can be compensated by higher intake, blending of protein sources, or fortification with limiting amino acids like leucine</cite> <cite id="fa31949a-4">When vegetarian diets increased protein to ~1.0–1.1 g/kg/day and matched meal composition (≥30 g/meal), muscle mass gains during resistance training in older men were similar to omnivorous diets; blending complementary plant proteins optimizes essential amino acid profiles</cite>.

Muscle protein synthesis across diet patterns
- Direct comparisons are scarce, but converging evidence shows that leucine-dense, high-quality protein sources (commoner in animal-heavy diets) acutely stimulate MPS, whereas plant-forward alkaline diets can achieve comparable MPS if amino acid/leucine intake per meal is sufficient. <cite id="da90c754-0">Leucine supplementation reverses impaired MPS in older adults, supporting the role of leucine as a potent stimulator via mTOR</cite> <cite id="e05199ed-4">Leucine-rich solution acutely increases human MPS and mTOR signaling and reduces AMPK, demonstrating robust translational activation</cite> <cite id="fa31949a-1">Alkaline diets have been reported to positively affect lean muscle mass in healthy older adults, suggesting plant-based patterns can support MPS when protein is adequate</cite>. 
- Quantity and timing are critical in older adults: suboptimal per-meal EAA/leucine loads (<~10 g total EAAs, <~2.5–2.8 g leucine per meal) blunt MPS, while meeting or exceeding these per meal and distributing protein across meals can preserve MPS despite a plant-forward pattern. <cite id="da90c754-0">Older adults show reduced response to lower EAA doses but BCAA/leucine administration restores synthesis rates</cite> <cite id="da90c754-4">Consuming at least ~2.5–2.8 g leucine per meal may help prevent sarcopenia in older people; several human studies show increases in skeletal muscle mass or functional measures with leucine-rich protein over months</cite>. 
- Animal models provide mechanistic support that lowering acid load and improving amino acid availability can favor muscle anabolism. <cite id="e05199ed-0">Protein restriction with leucine supplementation increased muscle FSR and mTOR signaling in rats</cite> <cite id="e05199ed-2">While some studies did not find increased skeletal muscle mass with chronic leucine, mechanistic work supports leucine’s regulation of MPS via mTOR and potential suppression of proteolysis via ubiquitin-proteasome or autophagy-lysosome inhibition</cite>.

- During aging and resistance training: when total daily protein is matched and per-meal plant proteins are adequately dosed and blended, plant-forward (alkaline-leaning) diets can produce similar muscle accretion as omnivorous diets; if protein is less dense or leucine-limited, omnivorous diets may yield greater gains, especially at lower training loads. <cite id="fa31949a-4">An omnivorous diet (1.0 g/kg/day) led to greater lean and muscle mass gains than a vegetarian diet (0.78 g/kg/day) during 12 weeks of resistance training in older men; when vegetarian protein was increased to ~1.1 g/kg/day, differences were reduced</cite> <cite id="fa31949a-4">Providing ≥30 g plant-based protein per meal enhanced lean mass accretion during prolonged resistance training in older adults</cite>.

- On muscle mass retention: when total protein is equated and older-adult-tailored strategies are used (adequate per-meal EAA/leucine, resistance exercise), alkaline/plant-based patterns perform comparably to traditional omnivorous patterns for maintaining or gaining muscle; when total protein is lower or per-meal leucine is insufficient on alkaline diets, traditional diets may yield better retention, especially during training or weight loss. <cite id="fa31949a-4">Omnivorous at 1.0 g/kg/day outperformed vegetarian 0.78 g/kg/day in training-induced muscle gains; increasing vegetarian protein to ~1.1 g/kg/day narrowed the gap</cite> <cite id="fa31949a-2">Vegan diets risk muscle loss unless protein and exercise are optimized; trials are testing whether resistance exercise offsets this</cite> <cite id="59bac8a5-3">Muscle accretion hinges on the balance of synthesis and degradation, both influenced by nutrition</cite>. 
- Role of exercise: resistance exercise amplifies MPS, attenuates protein breakdown, and interacts synergistically with protein quality/leucine; this often makes “traditional” protein sources more effective when training is present, but plant-based leucine-enriched proteins can still support gains. <cite id="da90c754-4">Proper resistance exercise improves muscle endurance, reduces myofibrillar MPS decreases during reduced stepping, and increases muscle mass and strength with leucine-rich protein over months</cite> <cite id="fa31949a-4">During prolonged resistance training, plant-based protein strategies (≥30 g/meal) can enhance lean mass accretion</cite>.

- For maximizing MPS and muscle retention across patterns:
  - Ensure per-meal EAAs and at least ~2.5–2.8 g leucine for older adults; distribute protein across multiple meals to avoid the postprandial “muscle-full” dampening. <cite id="da90c754-0">BCAAs/leucine restore MPS in older adults, with larger EAA doses (10–15 g, including ≥3 g leucine) restoring synthesis rates</cite> <cite id="da90c754-2">Supplemental leucine/EAA with meals lacking sufficient protein can enhance anabolism, but effects are blunted shortly after meals</cite>.

Title: Leucine Supplementation in a Chronically Protein-Restricted Diet Enhances Muscle Weight and Postprandial Protein Synthesis of Skeletal Muscle by Promoting the mTOR Pathway in Adult Rats
Snippet: Low protein intake causes a decrease in protein deposition in most animal tissues. The purpose of this study was to investigate whether leucine supplementation would increase the synthesis rate of protein and muscle weight in adult rats, which chronically consume only 58.8% of their protein requirements. Thirty-six male Sprague-Dawley rats were assigned to one of three dietary treatments including a 20% casein diet (CON), a 10% casein + 0.44% alanine diet (R), and a 10% casein + 0.87% leucine diet (RL). After a 10 d dietary treatment, plasma amino acid levels were measured after feeding, the gastrocnemius muscles and soleus muscles were harvested and weighed, and the fractional synthesis rate (FSR) and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling proteins in skeletal muscle were measured. Regarding the plasma amino acid level, the RL group had the highest concentration of leucine (P < 0.05) and the lowest concentration of isoleucine (P < 0.05) among the three groups, and the CON group had a lower concentration of valine (P < 0.05) than the R and RL groups. Compared with the R group, the RL group significantly increased in gastrocnemius muscle weight, protein synthesis rate, and phosphorylation of both ribosomal protein S6 kinase 1 (S6K1) and 4E-BP1. In conclusion, when protein is chronically restricted in adult rat diets, leucine supplementation moderately improves body weight gain and increases muscle protein synthesis through mTOR activation.

Leucine, isoleucine, and valine all contain a branched chain structure, so they are collectively called branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), and they are all essential amino acids. BCAAs have three main roles: as a raw material for protein synthesis, as a signaling molecule to stimulate protein synthesis, and to break down energy production during fasting (Le Couteur et al., 2020). Metabolism of BCAAs is concentrated in the muscle, and muscle tend to suffer from loss of quality and strength as the body ages. Reduced muscle anabolism and decreased response to insulin and amino acids in aging skeletal muscle, but still responsive to the administration of BCAAs, particularly leucine (Fujita and Volpi, 2006). Leucine can stimulate insulin secretion from beta cells in the pancreatic islets and work synergistically with glucose to regulate insulin secretion in response to dietary carbohydrate and protein intake (Neinast et al., 2019;Le Couteur et al., 2020). Studies have shown that a diet high in leucine can reverse the phenomenon of impaired muscle protein synthesis in the elderly, but the same diet had no significant effect on muscle protein synthesis in young adults (Katsanos et al., 2006). In addition, a study showed that skeletal muscle mass increased in the intervention group after dietary intervention with BCAA-rich supplements in patients with gait disorders, although there was no significant impact on daily activated (Moriwaki et al., 2019). However, it remains to be confirmed whether supplemental leucine can help older adults regain lost muscle mass. A systematic review and meta-analysis of leucine supplementation in older adults showed that leucine increased the rate of protein synthesis, but had no effect on lean body mass or lean leg mass in older adults (Xu et al., 2015).

Title: Effect of Intake of Leucine-Rich Protein Supplement in Parallel with Resistance Exercise on the Body Composition and Function of Healthy Adults
Snippet: Protein synthesis in skeletal muscle decreases with age, but is preserved when essential amino acids are ingested in more than the appropriate dose [9]. Specifically, leucine is one of the essential amino acids that cannot be synthesized in the body and can only be obtained through meat, fish, beans, or nuts. Leucine helps in skeletal muscle synthesis and protein balance by inducing the initiation of protein synthesis through an amino acid-sensing mechanism [10,11]. 

For effective protein synthesis in older people, consuming at least 2.5-2.8 g of leucine per meal may help prevent sarcopenia [12]. However, the results of the long-term use of leucine are still unclear. One study reported significant improvements in skeletal muscle mass in older people taking leucine-rich protein supplements for 3-4 months, but no muscle strength or functional changes were observed [13]. On the contrary, in a study of women living in Japan, no significant change was noted in skeletal muscle mass, but improvements in functions such as walking speed was noted [14]. In another study of healthy adults taking leucine-rich protein supplements for more than 8-16 months, skeletal muscle mass increased by 13-17% in areas including the arms and legs, and muscle strength was also improved [15]. In a study of older patients with type 2 diabetes, no significant changes were found in muscle function, body composition, or insulin sensitivity when consuming 2.5 g of leucine for ≥6 months [16]. 

Sarcopenia is caused by not only protein intake, but also increased muscle protein degradation and decreased muscle protein synthesis with age. Specifically, the decrease in activity increases resistance to stimulation for myofibrillar protein synthesis in the muscle [17]. In healthy older people, when the number of steps per day was reduced by approximately 76% for 2 weeks, insulin resistance increased by 12%, postprandial insulin sensitivity decreased by 43%, and myofibrillar protein synthesis decreased by 26% [18]. On the contrary, proper resistance exercise improves not only muscle strength but also muscular endurance, and positively affects body composition by affecting body fat reduction [19].

Protein synthesis in skeletal muscle decreases with age, but is preserved when essential amino acids are ingested in more than the appropriate dose [9]. Specifically, leucine is one of the essential amino acids that cannot be synthesized in the body and can only be obtained through meat, fish, beans, or nuts. Leucine helps in skeletal muscle synthesis and protein balance by inducing the initiation of protein synthesis through an amino acid-sensing mechanism [10,11]. 

For effective protein synthesis in older people, consuming at least 2.5-2.8 g of leucine per meal may help prevent sarcopenia [12]. However, the results of the long-term use of leucine are still unclear. One study reported significant improvements in skeletal muscle mass in older people taking leucine-rich protein supplements for 3-4 months, but no muscle strength or functional changes were observed [13]. On the contrary, in a study of women living in Japan, no significant change was noted in skeletal muscle mass, but improvements in functions such as walking speed was noted [14]. In another study of healthy adults taking leucine-rich protein supplements for more than 8-16 months, skeletal muscle mass increased by 13-17% in areas including the arms and legs, and muscle strength was also improved [15]. Sarcopenia is caused by not only protein intake, but also increased muscle protein degradation and decreased muscle protein synthesis with age. Specifically, the decrease in activity increases resistance to stimulation for myofibrillar protein synthesis in the muscle [17]. In healthy older people, when the number of steps per day was reduced by approximately 76% for 2 weeks, insulin resistance increased by 12%, postprandial insulin sensitivity decreased by 43%, and myofibrillar protein synthesis decreased by 26% [18]. Title: Leucine Supplementation in a Chronically Protein-Restricted Diet Enhances Muscle Weight and Postprandial Protein Synthesis of Skeletal Muscle by Promoting the mTOR Pathway in Adult Rats
Snippet: Low protein intake causes a decrease in protein deposition in most animal tissues. The purpose of this study was to investigate whether leucine supplementation would increase the synthesis rate of protein and muscle weight in adult rats, which chronically consume only 58.8% of their protein requirements. Thirty-six male Sprague-Dawley rats were assigned to one of three dietary treatments including a 20% casein diet (CON), a 10% casein + 0.44% alanine diet (R), and a 10% casein + 0.87% leucine diet (RL). After a 10 d dietary treatment, plasma amino acid levels were measured after feeding, the gastrocnemius muscles and soleus muscles were harvested and weighed, and the fractional synthesis rate (FSR) and mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling proteins in skeletal muscle were measured. Regarding the plasma amino acid level, the RL group had the highest concentration of leucine (P < 0.05) and the lowest concentration of isoleucine (P < 0.05) among the three groups, and the CON group had a lower concentration of valine (P < 0.05) than the R and RL groups. Compared with the R and RL groups, the CON group diet significantly increased (P < 0.05) feed intake, protein synthesis rate, and the phosphorylation of eukaryotic initiation factor 4E binding protein 1 (4E-BP1), and decreased the weight of abdominal adipose. Compared with the R group, the RL group significantly increased in gastrocnemius muscle weight, protein synthesis rate, and phosphorylation of both ribosomal protein S6 kinase 1 (S6K1) and 4E-BP1. In conclusion, when protein is chronically restricted in adult rat diets, leucine supplementation moderately improves body weight gain and increases muscle protein synthesis through mTOR activation.

Title: Differential effects of long-term leucine infusion on tissue protein synthesis in neonatal pigs
Snippet: Leucine is unique among the amino acids in its ability to promote protein synthesis by activating translation initiation via the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway. Previously, we showed that leucine infusion acutely stimulates protein synthesis in fast-twitch glycolytic muscle of neonatal pigs but this response cannot be maintained unless the leucine-induced fall in amino acids is prevented. Changes in the fractional rate of protein synthesis and activation of mTOR, as determined by eukaryotic initiation factor 4E binding protein (4E-BP1) and S6 kinase 1 (S6K1) phosphorylation, in the gastrocnemius and masseter muscles, heart, liver, jejunum, kidney, and pancreas were measured. Thus, long-term infusion of leucine stimulates mTOR signaling in skeletal muscle and some visceral tissues but the leucine-induced stimulation of protein synthesis in these tissues requires sustained amino acid availability.

Title: The effect of a vegan diet with or without resistance exercise on thigh muscle volume in older adults. Research protocol of the Vold-study: a 12-week randomized controlled trial
Snippet: Plant-based diets are increasingly adopted. Plant-based foods exhibit a lower protein quantity and quality compared to animal-based foods. As such, a fully plant-based, i.e. vegan, diet may be suboptimal for the maintenance of skeletal muscle mass later in life. The primary objectives of this study protocol are therefore: (1) To assess the effect of a 12-week self-composed vegan diet in comparison to an omnivorous diet on thigh muscle volume in community-dwelling older adults; and (2) To assess the effect of a 12-week self-composed vegan diet combined with twice-weekly resistance exercise (RE) on thigh muscle volume in comparison to a vegan diet without RE in community-dwelling older adults. Seventy-two community-dwelling individuals aged ≥ 65 years with a BMI between 23 and 32 kg/m2 will be included in this randomized controlled trial. Eligible participants will be randomly allocated to either follow their habitual omnivorous diet, a self-composed vegan diet, or a self-composed vegan diet combined with two sessions of RE per week for 12 weeks. Participants will be guided through monthly nutrition information meetings. Dietary intake and physical activity levels will be assessed using food records and accelerometery. The primary study outcome will be thigh muscle volume, assessed at baseline and after 12 weeks using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Secondary outcomes will be: body composition, muscle fat infiltration, muscle strength, bone mineral density, bone turnover markers, metabolic profile, insulin levels, cobalamin, iron and vitamin D status, hs-CRP, gut metabolomics and metagenomics, gastro-intestinal symptoms and dietary intake. Measurements will take place at baseline, after 6 weeks, and after 12 weeks. Additionally, mixed muscle protein synthesis rates will be assessed during the first ten days of the intervention using a deuterium oxide protocol. Data will be analysed using independent t-tests and linear mixed models. Additionally, mixed muscle protein synthesis rates will be assessed during the first ten days of the intervention using a deuterium oxide protocol. Data will be analysed using independent t-tests and linear mixed models. Summary
An alkaline-forming diet (rich in fruits and vegetables and lower in animal products and grains) is hypothesized to favor muscle mass retention by blunting diet-induced metabolic acidosis and by supplying cation-rich, antioxidant–rich foods, whereas “traditional” Western-style diets high in meat and grains are net acid–producing and can promote a mild acid load that increases muscle protein breakdown. In practice, both diet patterns differ in acid load and protein quality, and these differences influence muscle retention; preserving muscle during weight loss or caloric restriction benefits from adequate protein, leucine-rich sources, and resistance exercise, with alkali supplementation adding modest protection under energy-restricted or older-adult contexts. <cite id="7fc4da98-0">In normal adults, metabolic acidosis also stimulates nitrogen loss due to accelerated degradation of muscle protein, and a diet high in meats and grains promotes low-grade metabolic acidosis; alkali supplementation with potassium bicarbonate improved nitrogen balance in postmenopausal women with mild metabolic acidosis</cite> <cite id="7fc4da98-4">Higher alkaline dietary load has been positively associated with muscle mass indices, though the association weakens after controlling for protein percentage, and nutrients such as potassium, magnesium, and antioxidants in alkalinogenic foods may protect against oxidative stress and inflammation</cite> <cite id="9a483af1-0">Protein sources differ in acid/base potential: animal proteins and grains are net acid producers due to sulfur-containing amino acids, whereas fruits and vegetables are net base producers, and these differences can impact cellular pH homeostasis</cite> <cite id="9a483af1-1">Branched-chain amino acids, especially leucine, can enhance protein synthesis and inhibit degradation via mTOR signaling in human studies, though effects are not always consistent</cite> <cite id="f4b4aadf-2">Short-term potassium bicarbonate supplementation (60–120 mmol/day for 18 days) reduced urinary total nitrogen in postmenopausal women, suggesting potential preservation of muscle protein, with some reports of increased muscle performance, whereas effects in men were less evident</cite>.

Dietary acid load arises from metabolizable sulfur amino acids (animal proteins, grains) and phosphorus-rich foods, creating a net endogenous acid production that lowers intracellular pH and activates ubiquitin‑proteasome pathways (e.g., MURF1/MAFbx) and cathepsins, increasing net muscle protein degradation unless offset by sufficient anabolic signaling and amino acid availability. - Observational and cohort evidence: Greater adherence to a more alkaline diet pattern (higher fruit/vegetable intake, lower meat/dairy) correlates with better lean mass and muscle parameters, but associations attenuate when adjusting for protein percentage, highlighting that protein quantity/quality is a dominant driver. <cite id="7fc4da98-1">Alkaline diets have shown positive effects on lean muscle mass in healthy older adults, though evidence is limited</cite> <cite id="f4b4aadf-2">More alkaline diet patterns show slight positive associations with lean mass and muscle parameters in adult women; in a prospective cohort of ~3000 people, lower net endogenous acid production (NEAP) was linked to slower muscle mass wasting over four years</cite> <cite id="f4b4aadf-2">Higher alkaline dietary load was positively associated with muscle mass indices in Dawson-Hughes et al., but after controlling for protein percentage, the association became weaker</cite> <cite id="7fc4da98-4">Protein remains essential for muscle mass conservation, while alkalinogenic nutrients (potassium, magnesium, antioxidants) may add protection via oxidative stress and inflammation pathways</cite>.

Title: Leucine Supplementation in a Chronically Protein-Restricted Diet Enhances Muscle Weight and Postprandial Protein Synthesis of Skeletal Muscle by Promoting the mTOR Pathway in Adult Rats

Title: Post-Prandial Protein Handling: You Are What You Just Ate
